ingredients.name: wool fibres covered in microscopic overlapping scales
water and heat making the fibres swell and move
agitation pressing fibres past one another
irreversible interlocking

method: Soak the wool fibres and their scale-like outer surfaces in the wash: moisture makes the fibres swell, while heat and detergent can increase how freely they shift.
Add tumbling or rubbing and neighbouring fibres slide past one another; their scales catch, so the fibres migrate inward and lock together in a process called felting.
As more fibres interlock, the fabric becomes denser and occupies less area, which is why the garment looks shrunken even though individual fibres have not simply shortened like elastic.

evaporation at many temperatures versus a pressure-dependent boiling point
quiet loss versus sustained vapour bubbles

method: Difference one—where: evaporation removes faster-moving molecules only from the liquid's surface, while boiling forms vapour bubbles throughout the liquid.

Difference two—when: evaporation can happen at temperatures below the boiling point, while boiling begins when the liquid's vapour pressure matches the surrounding pressure at a characteristic temperature.
Difference three—what you see: evaporation is usually gradual without sustained bubbling in the body of the liquid, whereas boiling produces continuous bubbles that grow and rise.
